newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AWF boosts f'cst Australia wheat to 21.10 m/t.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AWF boosts f'cst Australia wheat to 21.10 m/t.

text.p: Private grains forecaster Australian Wheat Forecasters Pty Ltd (AWF) said on Thursday it had further increased its forecast for Australia's 1996/97 wheat production by almost 700,000 tonnes to 21.10 million tonnes.
AWF's previous forecast, issued last month, was 20.43 million tonnes. The latest forecast puts AWF at the upper end of the forecasting range in Australia.

The Australian Wheat Board (AWB) last week raised its forecast by one million tonnes to 21.0 million while the Australian government's Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics (ABARE) is forecasting 20.9 million tonnes.

AWF said in its latest forecast that further rain and cool conditions over the past month had increased the expected size of the incoming wheat crop. The wheat harvest had been in progress in Queensland for more than a month, it noted.
Early in November some wheat was showing signs of being rain affected and on receiveal was displaced into downgraded categories, it said.
Some growers had chosen to warehouse inferior wheats instead of delivering to the pool until the amount of weather damaged wheat in Australian eastern states could be assessed, it said.
As the harvest progressed in southern Queensland, the amount of weather damaged wheat presented at silos decreased, it said.

Rain fell throughout New South Wales over Monday and Tuesday of this week and wheat had just started to flow to silos in the northwest of the state, AWF said. Less than five percent of expected wheat had been received, it said.
Rain was typically 10 mm but stations such as Boomi had received 29 mm Bellata 23 mm.
Wednesday was a day of humid weather, it said.

The harvest had not yet started after the rain, but when it did the grain was still expected to be sound and of bright appearance, AWF said. However, there was a long way to go before the NSW harvest was complete, it noted.

On the balance of probabilities, a substantial quantity of wheat grown in the north of the state would be weather affected, it said. In the harvest of 1983 of 8 million tonnes delivered to the AWB within NSW, 3.4 million tonnes received into categories below Australian Standard White (ASW) quality, it said.
Early November 1996 rain which fell in the south of the state was favourable to wheat yields and neutral to quality because crops were still green, it said.
Victorian Mallee crops were expected to yield very well. There was a late frost but it was expected to have done more damage to barley than to wheat, it said.
The Victorian wheat harvest had not yet started, it said.
There had been some frost damage to some southern areas of the South Australian (SA) Mallee and a small crop of high quality wheat is expected.
There was a much lower probability of weather damaged wheat in SA because of the predominantly dry summer period, it said.
Western Australian crops had grown well despite a late start for the southern areas, it said.
The crops looked very well, but yield forecasts were modest because of the limited growing time that has been available.
